title: remembrance
hook: remembrance; a word repeated on the fingers, and the still watching (muraqaba) that sits beside it
tomorrow: a month of not-eating that's really a month of paying attention

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jumu'ah, Friday, gathering day. Your line was gather. Did you reach out to the person whose name came up? Day seventeen.

Watch someone's hands on a bus in Cairo, or Karachi, or Birmingham, Alabama. Sometimes the thumb is moving across the fingers, joint by joint, very lightly, while their lips move without sound. Or a string of beads is sliding through their fingers, one bead at a time, while they wait for their stop. They aren't counting money or steps. They're doing the thing the whole of Islam keeps circling back to. You met a piece of it on day three, alhamdulillah said after the prayer. Today, the practice behind it, and its quieter sister: saying nothing at all, and watching.
screen: `A THUMB ACROSS THE FINGERS.` → `BEADS ON THE BUS.` → `REMEMBRANCE, AND ITS QUIET SISTER.`

segments.voice: Dhikr. The root, dh-k-r, means to remember, and also to mention, to say aloud. In Arabic those are almost the same act: to remember someone is to bring their name up. The Qur'an even calls itself adh-dhikr, the reminder. And it makes a promise with this word. In Pickthall's words: “Therefore remember Me, I will remember you.” You remember, and you're remembered back. What does it sound like? Short phrases, said again and again. Subhan Allah: glory be to God. Alhamdulillah. Allahu akbar: God is greater. Hadith reports in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi describe the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ counting his dhikr on the fingers of his right hand, and telling people the fingers too will be asked, and will speak. Many Muslims use prayer beads, a misbaha; some scholars prefer the fingers, many are content with either. Now the quiet sister. In Islam's mystical tradition, Sufism, there's a practice called muraqaba, watchfulness, from r-q-b, to watch over. It rests on a famous hadith. A stranger in white asks the Prophet ﷺ: what is ihsan, doing it beautifully? The answer: to worship God as if you see Him; and if you don't see Him, He sees you. Sufi teachers built a sit on that line. Head a little lowered, eyes closed, watching the breath and the heart without chasing any thought. Underneath it is a verse, in Pickthall's words: “We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.” The formal sit belongs mostly to the Sufi orders, and some Muslims are wary of it. But both halves say the same thing. People forget. So you come back: with a word, or with silence.
screen: `DH-K-R — REMEMBER, AND MENTION.` · `COUNTED ON THE FINGERS.` · `MURAQABA — WATCHFULNESS.` · `AS IF YOU SEE HIM.` · then, large: `REMEMBER, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds, in two halves. First, rest your right hand open and touch your thumb to each joint of your fingers, slowly. With each touch, say a short phrase silently. If you pray, subhan Allah, or alhamdulillah. If not, one word you want to come back to: thanks, or peace. Then let your hand rest, lower your head a little, and just watch your breath, coming in and going out. When a thought swims past, see it, and let it go by. The bell holds the time.
Dhikr. Remembrance: short words of praise said again and again, and the quiet watching beside them. Seventeenth word.
Your line: remember, again. Pick one ordinary thing you do many times a day, unlocking your phone, opening a door, and let it be your cue to come back to one word, or one breath. Day seventeen.

howItsDone: Many Muslims say short phrases of dhikr after each prayer and through the day, counting on their fingers or on prayer beads. In many Sufi orders, dhikr is also chanted together, and muraqaba is a sitting practice of stillness, watching the heart and breath.

fork.setup: you're sitting with your dhikr, and your mind has wandered off to tomorrow's to-do list. what does the practice ask?
options: start the count over from zero.
come back to the next phrase.
stop until your mind is clear.
fork.reveal: dhikr is coming back. the wandering is the whole reason it's repeated.

original.note: Arabic: remembrance, and mention; the dh is said like the th in "this."

trapdoor: what you thought: repeating words like a chant.
what it means: dhikr, remembrance: short phrases said again and again, and a still watching beside them, so the heart keeps coming back.

what a scholar hears: dh-k-r joins remembering and mentioning; the Qur'an calls itself adh-dhikr; muraqaba, from r-q-b (ar-Raqib, the Watchful), is built on the answer about ihsan in the hadith of Jibril.
